name: Wildcat
seenIn: Covered in Football 101, Lesson 35: Gadget plays: the wildcat, the halfback pass and the pitch
what: The wildcat is a run play where the quarterback doesn't take the snap. The center snaps the ball straight to a running back or receiver lined up about five yards deep, and the quarterback lines up out wide like a receiver, as a decoy.

The math is the point. On a normal handoff the quarterback hands the ball off and stops playing, so the offense runs with ten players against eleven defenders. In the wildcat the runner takes the snap himself, so every offensive player is either blocking or carrying the ball: eleven against eleven. Often a tight end or extra lineman lines up on one side to add even more blockers.
Teams call it near the goal line and in short yardage, where one extra blocker matters most, and as a change of pace to catch a defense off guard.

caption: Dashed white: the direct snap from the center to the running back. Solid white: the back's run off the right side behind the tight end's block, and the receivers' routes; the quarterback is split out wide as a decoy.
spot: No one is under center or in the usual shotgun spot: the quarterback is split out wide near the sideline, and a running back or receiver stands alone about five yards behind the center. It shows up most inside the 5-yard line and on short-yardage downs.
beats: Defenses that can't match blockers to gaps in short yardage, because the offense gets an extra blocker. Log it as a Run in the drill: a wildcat look is a run the large majority of the time.
